paras: The shooting of Dick Wilson was the wounding of a Black steamboat worker by Constable Wetherhorn on the streets of Savannah, Georgia, on the afternoon of November 16, 1880. Wilson, who had escaped from a magistrate's office while under arrest, was hit in the left leg by the fifth of five shots fired during a chase toward the Bay and was taken to jail. The Savannah Morning News, the only paper found to report it, noted that the shooting set off public discussion of officers firing at prisoners on city streets.

Wilson, described as "a big, six-foot, strapping fellow," had worked for about ten days as an assistant to the engineer on the river steamer Katie. Magistrate Waring Russell Jr. had issued a warrant charging him with assault with intent to murder his wife, whom he was accused of beating with a heavy stick and kicking down the stairs.

At about five o'clock Wetherhorn found Wilson at the Katie's wharf and read him the warrant. According to the paper, Wilson struck the constable in the chest, said "I'm as good a man as you are," and walked off, saying he wanted the steamer's mate to sign his bond. Wetherhorn said several Black men gathered around him in a threatening manner, so he did not use force and instead followed Wilson until he got him to Russell's office on Bryan street.

There Wilson asked when he could be tried and told the constable to bring up the mate to sign his bond; when Wetherhorn refused, Wilson pushed past him and ran up Bryan street. The constable chased him down Whitaker street, fired once as he crossed Bay lane, and fired again as he ran along the north side of Bay street toward the Exchange. The fifth shot struck Wilson below the left knee in front of the Knickerbocker ice house, and he fell, was secured, and was carried to jail in a wagon. The wound was not considered serious, though the paper expected it to leave him limping for a while.

The paper said it was "informed" that Wilson had been drinking and that on the way to jail he said he was to blame and would have deserved to be badly wounded or killed; no statement of his own appears in the coverage. No report of a trial on the assault charge, an inquiry into the shooting, or action against the constable was found. In its year-end chronology of 1880 the Morning News listed the incident in one line under November 17 as "Dick alias Dock Johnson shot at by Constable Wetherhorn."

The Morning News ran the story under the headline "Exciting Chase After a Prisoner," telling it largely from the constable's side and printing his statement that he stayed calm and fired only where no one stood nearby. Its comment was mixed: it urged officers to try every other way of catching escaping prisoners before firing in the streets because of the danger to "innocent pedestrians," yet it called Wilson "insolent" and "a desperate character." The paper also reported that the gunfire drew people from every direction and that the danger of officers shooting at prisoners on public streets "was discussed with some feeling." No other paper's version of the shooting was found, and the later chronology entry gave the man's surname as Johnson.

reader.title: Shooting of Dick Wilson
bases: A constable fired five shots at an escaping Black prisoner on Savannah's streets and wounded him in the leg; no crowd took part (A4).
Only the Savannah Morning News reported the shooting, in one detailed account (A4) and a one-line entry in its own year-end chronology (A12), which are not independent.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News local report, partly from the constable
accounts.gist: Wilson struck the constable at the wharf, later bolted from the magistrate's office, and was brought down by the fifth shot; Wetherhorn said Black men at the wharf were threatening and that he fired only where the street was empty.

accounts.label: Statements attributed to Wilson (unnamed informants)
accounts.gist: The paper was 'informed' that Wilson had been drinking and said on the way to jail that he was to blame and would have deserved to be killed.

framing.detail: The Morning News called Wilson 'insolent' and 'a desperate character' and printed the constable's defense, but also warned that firing at escaping prisoners on the streets endangered 'innocent pedestrians'.

conflicts.note: The contemporaneous report is fuller and closer to the event; the chronology entry matches it on given names, constable and date.
The chronology indexes stories by issue date, so November 17 is the publication date of A4.
